findings: ScalarReadWorkspace owns its returned reservations independently of scope disposal. Closing its parent stage during comparison does not release active scalar storage prematurely.
Closing a scope from the decoder callback leaves the in-progress scalar charged; workspace detects closure, rejects before decoding the next scalar, and releases at settlement.

Materialization cache references point to strings already covered by mandatory output admission. Top-k comparison strings instead use reusable two-value scratch and cannot safely be retained in that reference-only cache.

newCases: Parent-stage disposal inside comparison: both values remain usable; a sibling cannot reserve one byte until callback returns; final cleanup is zero.
Scope disposal inside decode: current scalar stays charged during callback; second decode never begins; typed disposal failure and final zero cleanup.

topKReuseContract: Retained decoded keys must have separate payload admission, including string storage and reference/index bookkeeping.
Optional retained keys must relinquish capacity before a mandatory wider scalar read or gather would otherwise fail; preserve direct-access success at exact boundaries.
Do not evict shared transport caches merely to prepare keys. Preparation must be bounded by available parent/query/pool allowances.
Cache lifetime must end before result gather unless output intentionally retains an independently charged owner; borrowed binary and mutable nested values cannot share immutable-text cache semantics.
Measure reuse under actual mixed selections and concurrency before selecting a default. Existing eager-preparation benchmarks are insufficient evidence for universal preparation.
remaining: F5 adaptive top-k preparation and broader allocation/runtime audit remain open.
